meta.audience: The peaceable followers of Christ in the church
meta.location: A synagogue they had built for the place of worship
meta.date: Mormon's sermon, copied out by Moroni after AD 400
meta.unit: Mormon on faith, hope, and charity (Moroni 7)
principles: Three named things taken in order

world_behind.title: Moroni is copying his father
world_behind.text: Verse 1 says he writes a few of the words of Mormon.

world_behind.title: The setting is a building
world_behind.text: Verse 1 names a synagogue they had built for worship.

world_behind.title: The audience is inside the church
world_behind.text: Verse 3 addresses those who have already obtained a sufficient hope by which they can enter into the rest of the Lord. Verse 1 says the sermon was given in a synagogue which they had built for a place of worship, so this is Mormon preaching inside a functioning congregation rather than to a nation in collapse.

world_behind.title: He judges them by how they walk
world_behind.text: Verse 4 gives their peaceable walk with the children of men as his reason for judging them. Moroni 9:18 and 20 has him describe the same people's countrymen as without order, without mercy, and past feeling, so both descriptions belong to the same lifetime.

world_behind.title: The parts are announced in advance
world_behind.text: Verse 1 lists the three subjects, and the sermon works through them in that order.

world_behind.title: The miracle question is put three times
world_behind.text: Verses 27, 29, and 35 each ask again whether miracles have ceased. Mormon 9:15 to 20 puts the same question five more times in his own voice, and 2 Nephi 28:6 predicts the doctrine that they have. Father and son argue the point across two books.

world_behind.title: The ending is a request
world_behind.text: Verse 48 asks them to pray with all the energy of heart to be filled with the love just described. 1 Corinthians 13:4 to 8 is the passage verses 45 and 46 track almost clause for clause, and Moroni 7:48 goes past it by turning the description into an instruction.

words.text: A building for assembly and worship. Treated at Alma 16:13. It appears four times in the record and forty-five in the King James Bible. Verse 1 says the people had built this one themselves.
Unwillingly, while resenting the cost. It appears once in the record, here, and once in the King James Bible, at 2 Corinthians 9:7.
Draws a person on by appeal. The record uses the word three times, twice in this chapter, and the King James Bible once. Verses 12 and 13 use it of both sides.
To ask urgently. Treated at Jacob 6:5. The record uses the word four times and the King James Bible sixty-seven.
Pleads a case on another's behalf. It shows up once in the record, here, and nowhere in the King James Bible.
Likeness to God in conduct. The word appears once in the record, here, and fifteen times in the King James Bible. Verse 30 says angels show themselves to those who have it.
Comes to an end, or gives out. One use in the record, here, against nineteen in the King James Bible, including 1 Corinthians 13:8.

phrases.term: In the synagogue which they had built for the place of worship
phrases.text: Where the sermon was given. Moroni supplies the room before the words.

phrases.term: By their works ye shall know them
phrases.text: The rule Mormon starts from. 3 Nephi 14:16 has the Lord give it as fruits.

phrases.term: Except he shall do it with real intent it profiteth him nothing
phrases.text: The condition on a gift or a prayer. Verse 8 works out what that means.

phrases.term: A bitter fountain cannot bring forth good water
phrases.text: The figure for the rule. The verse runs it both directions before applying it.

phrases.term: Inviteth and enticeth to do good continually
phrases.text: The mark of what comes from God. Verse 12 gives the opposite in the same words.

phrases.term: As plain, that ye may know with a perfect knowledge, as the daylight is from the dark night
phrases.text: Mormon's claim about how hard the judging is. He puts the difficulty at nearly zero.

phrases.term: If ye will lay hold upon every good thing, and condemn it not
phrases.text: The instruction that follows the tool. Verse 20 then asks how it can be done.

phrases.term: It is by faith that miracles are wrought
phrases.text: The answer to the question asked three times. Verse 37 turns their absence into a diagnosis.

phrases.term: Without faith there cannot be any hope
phrases.text: The order set between the first two. Verse 43 adds meekness underneath both.

phrases.term: Charity is the pure love of Christ
phrases.text: The definition given after the description. Verse 45 had listed what it does.

phrases.term: Pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart
phrases.text: What Mormon asks of them at the end. The love is something to be given rather than worked up.

verses.label: v. 1–2
verses.title: Two first persons in two verses, and a building named
verses.text: The record hands the page over with an explicit note: "I, Moroni, write a few of the words of my father Mormon," and the very next verse opens "I, Mormon, speak unto you." The switch is marked, not silent. Verse 1 also supplies a setting that nothing in the sermon requires, "as he taught them in the synagogue which they had built for the place of worship." A sermon reaching the reader through a son's transcription is given a room and an audience before it is given a topic.

verses.label: v. 5–10
verses.title: One test stated, then run twice with the same result
verses.text: The record quotes the rule, "by their works ye shall know them," which stands at Matthew 7:16 and 7:20, and then applies it to two specific acts. A gift given grudgingly "is counted unto him the same as if he had retained the gift." A prayer offered "not with real intent of heart" likewise "profiteth him nothing." The phrase "real intent" appears twice and "it profiteth him nothing" twice. The record thus takes a maxim about recognizing others and turns it into a test of the giver's interior state, which is the opposite direction from the source.

verses.label: v. 27–38
verses.title: One question asked four times
verses.text: The record returns to the same challenge at verses 27, 29, 35, and 36, rephrasing it each time: "have miracles ceased," "have miracles ceased," "has the day of miracles ceased," and then a run of three, "have angels ceased to appear," "has he withheld the power of the Holy Ghost," "or will he, so long as time shall last." The answer "Nay" is given twice. The position being attacked is quoted directly at 2 Nephi 28:6, "this day he is not a God of miracles," and argued against again at Mormon 9:15–20. The record raises the same objection three times across three books and never lets it stand.

chapter.title: The sermon is arranged in three announced parts
chapter.text: Verse 1 names faith, hope, and charity, and verses 21, 40, and 44 take them in that order.

chapter.title: The test is what a thing moves you toward
chapter.text: Verses 13 and 16 both judge by whether something invites and entices to do good.

chapter.title: Intent decides what the act is worth
chapter.text: Verses 6 through 9 count a grudging gift the same as a gift kept back.

chapter.title: The judging is described as easy
chapter.text: Verse 15 sets the difficulty at telling daylight from dark night.

chapter.title: The tool comes with a warning
chapter.text: Verse 18 says the same judgment used will be used on the judge.

chapter.title: One question is asked three times
chapter.text: Verses 27, 29, and 35 put the miracle question again each time.

chapter.title: Their absence would be a diagnosis
chapter.text: Verses 37 and 38 make ceased miracles a report on unbelief.

chapter.title: The three are stacked on each other
chapter.text: Verse 42 hangs hope on faith, verse 43 hangs both on meekness, and verse 44 puts charity on top.

applications.title: Give with real intent
applications.text: The test is applied to two ordinary acts, a gift and a prayer, and both fail the same way. A gift given grudgingly "is counted unto him the same as if he had retained the gift." Before the next thing you do reluctantly for someone, decide whether you would rather not do it at all.

applications.title: Check what a thing moves you toward
applications.text: The test offered is whether it "inviteth and enticeth to do good, and to love God, and to serve him," and verse 17 gives the mirror image for the other direction. Apply it to something you are unsure about by asking what it has actually moved you to do this month.

applications.title: Judge in the direction the test works
applications.text: The claim is absolute in one direction only: the devil "persuadeth no man to do good, no, not one." That makes a good outcome usable as evidence and a bad one much less so. Be slower to condemn a source than to credit one.

applications.title: Use the measure you want used on you
applications.text: The verse attaches your judgment to your own case, "with that same judgment which ye judge ye shall also be judged." Decide the standard while you are still thinking about somebody else, and then apply it to yourself first.

applications.title: Lay hold on every good thing and condemn it not
applications.text: The instruction has two halves and the second is the harder one. Take something good you have been withholding approval from because of where it came from, and stop.

applications.title: Ask whether the objection has already been answered
applications.text: The chapter puts the same question four times, "have miracles ceased," and answers it with a reason rather than an assertion: "it is by faith that miracles are wrought." When you have been asked something repeatedly, that is a sign your answer has not yet included its ground.

applications.title: Do not assume you have the whole list
applications.text: The description of charity here runs to thirteen items where 1 Corinthians 13 gives fifteen, and the two missing ones are about self-display. Read a list you know well against its source occasionally; what has dropped out is worth noticing.

applications.title: Ask to be filled
applications.text: Mormon ends by telling them to "pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love." After forty-seven verses of analysis the instruction is to ask for the thing rather than to produce it.

questions.text: What do my works say about me this month?
Which fountain am I drawing from?
Where do I claim a thing is hard to judge when it is not?
What judgment have I made that I would hate to have applied to me?
Am I meek enough for charity to be possible?
What would praying with all the energy of heart look like?
